slides.heading: Light – Reflection and Refraction
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how curved mirrors form images, and how to find those images with simple ray diagrams.

nodes.label: Images: real or virtual, big or small

visual.alt: Flow from light travelling in straight lines to reflection, curved mirrors and the images they form

slides.narration: Namaste! Look into a shiny steel spoon. On one side your face appears upside down; on the other it is upright but tiny. Why? The answer lies in how curved surfaces reflect light. In this part we learn the language of spherical mirrors and a powerful tool, the ray diagram, which lets us predict exactly where an image will form.

slides.heading: Reflection: the two laws
slides.body_md: Light falling on a polished surface is reflected. **(1)** The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. **(2)** The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. These laws hold for **all** reflecting surfaces, flat or curved.

rows: As far behind the mirror as the object is in front

visual.alt: Table of the properties of the image formed by a plane mirror

slides.narration: You met these laws in earlier classes with plane mirrors. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and everything lies in one plane. A plane mirror gives an upright, same-size image that seems to be behind the mirror. The exciting part is that the very same laws apply at every tiny point of a curved mirror. That is all we need to explain spherical mirrors.

slides.heading: Spherical mirrors: concave and convex
slides.body_md: A **spherical mirror** is part of a hollow sphere. If the reflecting surface curves **inwards** (like the inside of a spoon), it is **concave**. If it bulges **outwards** (like the back of a spoon), it is **convex**.

visual.alt: Table comparing concave and convex mirrors by reflecting surface, effect on parallel rays and an everyday example

slides.narration: Imagine cutting a piece out of a hollow, shiny ball. If you look into the inside, you have a concave mirror; it curves inwards like a cave, which is an easy way to remember the name. If you look at the outside, you have a convex mirror, bulging out towards you. Concave mirrors bring light together; convex mirrors spread it out.

slides.heading: Pole, centre of curvature and focus
slides.body_md: The **pole (P)** is the centre of the mirror’s surface. The **centre of curvature (C)** is the centre of the sphere it is part of; the **radius of curvature (R)** is the distance PC. The **principal axis** passes through P and C. Rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to meet (convex) at the **principal focus (F)**; **PF** is the **focal length (f)**. For mirrors of small aperture, $R = 2f$.

slides.narration: Learn these points well, because every ray diagram uses them. P is on the mirror itself. C is the centre of the imaginary sphere, so it lies in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex one. F lies exactly halfway between P and C. So if the radius of curvature is forty centimetres, the focal length is twenty centimetres.

slides.heading: Rules for drawing ray diagrams
slides.body_md: Any **two** of these rays fix the image. Each follows the laws of reflection.

rows: Through F (or towards F for convex)
Through C (or towards C for convex)
Reflects at an equal angle on the other side of the axis
Reflects at an equal angle on the other side of the axis

visual.alt: Table of four standard incident rays and how a concave and a convex mirror reflect each

slides.narration: Here is the toolkit. A ray parallel to the axis reflects through the focus. A ray through the focus reflects parallel. A ray through the centre of curvature hits the mirror head-on, along the normal, so it comes straight back. A ray striking the pole bounces off at an equal angle. Pick any two, find where they meet, and that is your image.

slides.heading: Concave mirror: object at infinity
slides.body_md: Rays from a very distant object, such as the Sun, arrive **parallel** to the axis. After reflection they **meet at F**. The image is at **F**: real, inverted and **point-sized**.

slides.narration: Sunlight arrives in parallel rays because the Sun is so far away. A concave mirror gathers these rays to a single bright point, the focus. That is why the focus is so hot in a solar cooker. Never look at this point directly, and never point a mirror at a person’s eyes, because concentrated sunlight can burn.

slides.narration: Now bring the object closer, but keep it beyond the centre of curvature. Follow the two rays from the tip of the object. Where they cross, below the axis, is the tip of the image. It forms between F and C, upside down and smaller. Because the rays really meet there, the image is real: you could catch it on a screen.

slides.narration: Place a small bulb exactly at the focus and the mirror sends out a parallel beam. That is how torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights throw light a long way without spreading out much. In ray-diagram language, the reflected rays never meet, so we say the image forms at infinity.

slides.narration: Bring your face very close to a concave shaving or make-up mirror and you see a big, upright image of yourself. The reflected rays spread apart, and your eyes trace them back to a point behind the mirror. No light actually reaches that point, so the image is virtual. Dashed lines in a ray diagram always show these backward extensions.

slides.heading: Concave mirror images: the full table
slides.body_md: As the object moves from far away towards the mirror, the image moves from F out to infinity and becomes larger; inside F it becomes virtual and erect.

visual.alt: Table of image position, size and nature for six object positions in front of a concave mirror

slides.narration: This table is one of the most tested ideas in the chapter. Notice the pattern. Every real image is inverted, and the only virtual image, when the object is inside F, is erect and enlarged. Learn the table as a story of an object walking towards the mirror, and the image running the other way, growing all the time.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: positioning the object
slides.body_md: Ananya wants to use a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm to throw an **enlarged, real** image of a candle flame onto a wall. Where should she place the candle? Where should she place it to see an **enlarged, upright** image in the mirror instead?
bullets: Step 1 — R = 2f = 30 cm, so C is 30 cm and F is 15 cm from the mirror.
Step 2 — Enlarged and real: the object must be **between C and F**, that is, between 15 cm and 30 cm from the mirror.
Step 3 — Enlarged and upright (virtual): the object must be **between F and P**, closer than 15 cm.
Check — real images are always inverted, so the flame on the wall will appear upside down.

visual.alt: Worked table: for an enlarged real image place the object between 15 and 30 centimetres; for an enlarged upright image place it closer than 15 centimetres

slides.narration: Start by turning the focal length into the positions of F and C. Then use the table: enlarged real images need the object between C and F, and enlarged upright images need it inside F. Notice that the flame on the wall will be upside down. Every real image formed by a single mirror is inverted, which is a quick way to check your answers.

slides.body_md: For a convex mirror, the reflected rays always **diverge**. Extended backwards, they meet behind the mirror, **between P and F**. The image is always **virtual, erect and diminished**, wherever the object is.

visual.caption: Drawn to scale from the mirror or lens formula: every ray meets at the image point.

slides.narration: A convex mirror is simple to remember: whatever you do, the image is upright, smaller, and seems to be just behind the mirror. As the object moves closer, the image grows a little but never becomes as large as the object. Because it squeezes a wide view into a small image, a convex mirror shows you a lot of the scene at once.

slides.heading: Uses of spherical mirrors
slides.body_md: Each mirror is chosen for the kind of image or beam it produces.

rows: Bulb at F gives a strong parallel beam
Face inside F gives an enlarged, erect image
Erect image and a wide field of view

visual.alt: Table of uses of concave and convex mirrors with the reason for each

slides.narration: Next time you travel, notice the mirrors around you. The headlights of the bus use concave reflectors with the bulb at the focus. The driver’s side mirrors are convex, giving an upright view of a wide stretch of road behind. At the dentist, a small concave mirror shows your teeth enlarged. Every use comes straight from the ray diagrams.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which mirror for the job?
slides.body_md: Choose a mirror for each job and justify: (a) a truck driver’s side mirror, (b) a mirror to examine a small splinter in a finger, (c) a reflector for a powerful torch.
bullets: Step 1 — (a) **Convex**: always gives an erect, diminished image, so a wide area of road fits in the mirror.
Step 2 — (b) **Concave**, with the finger closer than F: an enlarged, erect, virtual image.
Step 3 — (c) **Concave**, with the bulb at F: the reflected rays form a parallel beam.
Check — each choice matches a row of the image table.

visual.alt: Worked table matching three jobs to convex or concave mirrors with object positions and the image or beam produced

slides.narration: Exam questions often hide the mirror choice inside a situation. Ask yourself what the user needs: a wide upright view, an enlarged view, or a parallel beam. A wide view always means convex. Enlarged and upright means concave with the object very close. A beam means concave with the source at the focus. Always give the reason as well as the name.

slides.heading: Quick check: the rear-view mirror
slides.body_md: Why are convex mirrors used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles?
slides.narration: Your turn. Think about what a driver needs to see behind, and what kind of image a convex mirror always gives.

slides.heading: Summary: spherical mirrors
bullets: Laws of reflection hold for curved mirrors too.
P, C, F and the principal axis; R = 2f.
Ray rules: parallel → through F; through F → parallel; through C → back on itself.
Concave: real and inverted images except when the object is inside F (virtual, erect, enlarged).
Convex: always virtual, erect and diminished, between P and F.
Uses: concave for beams, shaving, dentists, solar cookers; convex for rear-view mirrors.

rows: Real inverted (any size) or virtual erect enlarged

visual.alt: Summary table of the kinds of image a concave and a convex mirror can form

slides.narration: Let us recap. Spherical mirrors obey the same laws of reflection as plane mirrors. With a few standard rays you can find any image. Concave mirrors are versatile: they give real images of many sizes, or a big upright image when the object is very close. Convex mirrors always give small, upright images, which is perfect for watching the road behind.

slides.heading: Exam tips: ray diagrams
bullets: Use a ruler, draw **arrows** on every ray, and mark **P, F, C** on the axis.
Two rays are enough; choose the easiest pair for the object position.
Draw virtual rays and virtual images with **dashed** lines.
Always state the image’s **position, size and nature** (real or virtual, erect or inverted).
Do not draw a convex mirror’s focus in front of it: F and C are behind a convex mirror.
Typical 3-mark split: correct rays (1) + image drawn (1) + position, size and nature stated (1).

rows: Every ray needs an arrow showing direction
Virtual image drawn with solid lines
Use dashed lines for virtual rays and images
Convex mirror images are always diminished
Real images from a single mirror are inverted

visual.alt: Table of common ray-diagram mistakes and the correct ideas

slides.narration: Ray diagrams carry easy marks if you are neat. Use a sharp pencil and a ruler, put arrowheads on every ray, and dash the virtual parts. Label P, F and C. Then describe the image in words: where it is, how big it is, and whether it is real or virtual, erect or inverted. Examiners look for all three descriptions.

decks.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction — Part 2: Sign convention and the mirror formula
goals: Apply the New Cartesian sign convention to spherical mirrors
Use the mirror formula to find image distance, object distance or focal length
Calculate magnification and interpret its sign and size

slides.heading: Mirror formula and magnification
slides.body_md: Part 2 — turning ray diagrams into numbers with a sign convention and one simple formula.

visual.alt: Flow from the sign convention to the mirror formula, image distance, magnification and the nature of the image

slides.narration: Ray diagrams tell us roughly where an image forms. But an optician or an engineer needs exact numbers. In this part you will learn a sign convention and one neat formula that together give the position and size of any image formed by a spherical mirror, with signs that even tell you whether the image is real or virtual.

slides.heading: The New Cartesian sign convention
slides.body_md: The **pole** is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis. The object is placed to the **left**, so incident light travels left to right. Distances measured **in the direction of the incident light** are **positive**; distances measured **against** it are **negative**. Heights **above** the axis are **positive**; heights **below** are **negative**.

slides.narration: Think of the pole as the zero mark on a number line. Light comes from the left, so anything to the left of the mirror, including the object, has a negative distance. Anything behind the mirror, to the right, is positive. Heights work like a graph: up is positive, down is negative. Write these signs down before you do any calculation.

slides.heading: What the signs tell you
slides.body_md: Once the convention is fixed, the signs of the answers carry meaning.

rows: Negative if real; positive if virtual
Negative if real and inverted; positive if virtual and erect

visual.alt: Table of the signs of object distance, focal length, image distance and magnification for concave and convex mirrors

slides.narration: Here is the decoding key. For a mirror, the object distance is always negative because the object is in front. A concave mirror’s focus is in front too, so its focal length is negative. A convex mirror’s focus is behind, so its focal length is positive. If your image distance comes out negative, the image is in front and real; if positive, it is behind and virtual.

slides.heading: The mirror formula and magnification
slides.body_md: The **mirror formula** links object distance $u$, image distance $v$ and focal length $f$. **Magnification** $m$ is the ratio of image height $h'$ to object height $h$.

visual.alt: Table explaining what a negative or positive magnification and a size greater or less than one mean

slides.narration: Two formulas do all the work. The mirror formula says one over v plus one over u equals one over f. The magnification is the image height over the object height, which also equals minus v over u. A negative magnification means the image is upside down and real. A size bigger than one means the image is enlarged. The derivation is not required; using it correctly is.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: concave mirror
slides.body_md: An object 4 cm tall is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image.
bullets: Step 1 — Signs: $u = -15\ \text{cm}$, $f = -10\ \text{cm}$, $h = +4\ \text{cm}$.
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30\ \text{cm}$.
Step 3 — $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-30}{-15} = -2$, so $h' = m \times h = -2 \times 4 = -8\ \text{cm}$.
Conclusion — the image is 30 cm **in front** of the mirror, **real, inverted** and **enlarged** (8 cm tall).

rows: In front of the mirror: real

visual.alt: Worked table: image distance minus 30 centimetres, magnification minus 2, image height minus 8 centimetres

slides.narration: Follow the same routine every time. First write each quantity with its sign. Then rearrange the formula to find one over v, and combine the fractions carefully. Finally use the magnification to find the image height. Check the answer against the ray diagram: the object is between C and F here, so the image should be beyond C, real, inverted and enlarged. It is.

slides.heading: Quick check: image distance
slides.body_md: Solve the numerical question about a concave mirror.
slides.narration: Your turn. Write u and f with their signs first, then use one over v equals one over f minus one over u. Watch your signs carefully.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: convex mirror
slides.body_md: A car’s convex side mirror has a focal length of 20 cm. A motorcycle is 30 cm from the mirror (in a model set-up). Find the image distance and magnification.
bullets: Step 1 — Signs: $u = -30\ \text{cm}$, $f = +20\ \text{cm}$ (convex).
Conclusion — the image is 12 cm **behind** the mirror, **virtual, erect** and **diminished** (0.4 times the size).

visual.caption: Drawn to scale from the mirror or lens formula: every ray meets at the image point.

slides.narration: For a convex mirror the focal length is positive, because the focus is behind the mirror. Substituting carefully, the image distance comes out positive, which means the image is behind the mirror and virtual. The magnification is positive and less than one, so the image is upright and smaller. That matches the convex mirror rule exactly.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the object distance
slides.body_md: A dentist wants an **erect** image of a tooth that is **3 times** larger, using a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. How far from the tooth should the mirror be held?
bullets: Step 1 — Erect means virtual, so $m = +3 = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, giving $v = -3u$.
Step 2 — Substitute in $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$: $-\dfrac{1}{3u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{12}$, so $\dfrac{2}{3u} = -\dfrac{1}{12}$.
Step 3 — $3u = -24$, so $u = -8\ \text{cm}$, and $v = -3u = +24\ \text{cm}$.
Check — the tooth is 8 cm away, inside F (12 cm), so the image is virtual and erect, as required.

visual.alt: Worked table: magnification plus 3, object distance minus 8 centimetres, image distance plus 24 centimetres

slides.narration: Sometimes the question gives the magnification and asks for the object distance. Use the magnification to connect v and u, then substitute into the mirror formula, leaving only u. Here the tooth must be eight centimetres from the mirror, which is inside the focus, just as the ray diagram rule for an enlarged upright image predicts.

slides.heading: How the image moves as the object moves
slides.body_md: For a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, the graph shows the image distance for objects placed beyond F. As the object approaches F, the image rushes away towards infinity; far-away objects form images close to F.

points.label: Object at C: image at C

visual.alt: Graph of image distance against object distance for a concave mirror of focal length 10 centimetres: the curve falls from very large values near 10 centimetres, passes through 20 and 20, and approaches 10 centimetres for distant objects
visual.caption: Distances are sizes only (without signs); the curve is the mirror formula.

slides.narration: This graph shows the mirror formula as a picture. Start far away on the right: the image is just outside the focus. Move the object closer, and the image moves out. At twenty centimetres, which is C, object and image are at the same place. Just outside the focus, the image shoots off towards infinity. The graph explains the whole image table at a glance.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the sign of m
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the magnification produced by a convex mirror.
slides.narration: Quick check. What sign and size of magnification does a convex mirror always give? Then decide whether the reason explains it.

slides.heading: Signs at a glance: concave versus convex
slides.body_md: Keep this comparison handy while solving numericals.
columns:
**Concave mirror**

- f negative
- Real image: v negative, m negative
- Virtual image (object inside F): v positive, m positive and greater than 1

**Convex mirror**

- f positive
- Image always virtual: v positive
- m positive and less than 1

rows: In front of the mirror, real

visual.alt: Table for interpreting the sign of the image distance and magnification

slides.narration: Here is your sign summary in one place. A concave mirror has a negative focal length; a convex mirror a positive one. If v is negative, the image is in front and real; if positive, behind and virtual. If m is negative, the image is inverted; if positive, erect. Always end a numerical by translating your signs into words.

slides.heading: Quick check: radius and focus
slides.body_md: A spherical mirror has a radius of curvature of 32 cm. What is its focal length?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the simple relation between the radius of curvature and the focal length.

slides.heading: Summary: mirror formula
bullets: Pole = origin; incident light from the left; along the light positive, against it negative.
Mirror formula: $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$; $R = 2f$.
Magnification: $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u}$.
Concave: f negative. Convex: f positive. Object distance u is negative for real objects.
v negative → real; v positive → virtual. m negative → inverted; m positive → erect.

visual.alt: Summary table of the mirror formula and two forms of magnification with their uses

slides.narration: Let us recap. Fix the sign convention first, then use one over v plus one over u equals one over f, and m equals minus v over u. The signs of your answers describe the image: where it is, whether it is real or virtual, and whether it is upright or inverted. Practise a few problems every day and this becomes automatic.

slides.heading: Exam tips: mirror numericals
bullets: Write **given** values with signs, then the **formula**, then **substitution**, then the **answer with unit**.
Never drop the minus sign of a concave mirror’s focal length.
Combine fractions carefully; find 1/v first, then invert.
Finish with a sentence: position, nature (real or virtual, erect or inverted) and size.
Check the answer against the ray-diagram table.
Typical 3-mark split: signs and formula (1) + correct v (1) + m with nature of the image (1).

rows: Taking f positive for a concave mirror
f is negative for a concave mirror
State real or virtual from the sign of v

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in mirror numericals with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Most lost marks in numericals come from signs. Write every given value with its sign before touching the formula. Find one over v, then remember to turn it upside down. For mirrors, magnification has a minus sign: minus v over u. Finally, write a sentence describing the image. A correct number with no interpretation rarely earns full marks.

decks.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction — Part 3: Refraction of light
goals: State the laws of refraction and trace a ray through a rectangular glass slab
Calculate absolute and relative refractive index from speeds of light

slides.heading: Refraction of light
slides.body_md: Part 3 — why light bends when it passes from one medium into another, and how we measure that bending.

visual.alt: Flow showing light reaching a new medium, changing speed and therefore changing direction

slides.narration: Put a pencil in a glass of water and it looks broken at the surface. A coin at the bottom of a bucket seems closer than it is. A lemon in a glass of water looks bigger. All these tricks are caused by refraction, the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another. Let us find out why it happens and how to measure it.

slides.heading: What is refraction?
slides.body_md: Light travels at **different speeds** in different media. When it passes **obliquely** from one transparent medium into another, its speed changes and so does its **direction**. This change of direction is **refraction**.

rows: Pencil looks bent at the water surface
Light from the submerged part bends as it leaves water
Bottom of a pond looks shallower
Rays bend away from the normal as they leave water
Letters look raised under a glass block
Lemon looks larger in a glass of water
The curved glass and water bend light like a lens

visual.alt: Table of four everyday observations caused by refraction

slides.narration: Imagine a column of marching students crossing from a smooth road onto sand at an angle. The students who reach the sand first slow down, while the others are still on the road, so the whole column swings round. Light does the same when one side of a beam slows down before the other. A change in speed, at an angle, means a change in direction.

slides.heading: Refraction through a glass slab
slides.body_md: Entering glass from air, the ray bends **towards** the normal (r < i). Leaving glass into air, it bends **away** from the normal. In a slab with parallel faces, the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray**, but shifted sideways: the **lateral shift**.

slides.narration: In the lab, you trace a ray through a rectangular glass slab with pins. On entering glass, light slows down and bends towards the normal. On leaving, it speeds up and bends away by exactly the same amount, because the two faces are parallel. So the light comes out travelling in its original direction, just shifted sideways. The angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence.

slides.heading: The laws of refraction
slides.body_md: **(1)** The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the **same plane**. **(2)** For a given pair of media and a given colour of light, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is **constant** (**Snell’s law**). This constant is the **refractive index** of the second medium with respect to the first.

visual.alt: Table of the direction of bending when light passes between optically rarer and denser media

slides.narration: The first law is like reflection: everything stays in one plane. The second law, Snell’s law, says that for two given materials, sine of i divided by sine of r is always the same number, whatever the angle. That number is the refractive index. Notice also that a ray hitting the surface straight on, along the normal, passes through without bending.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using Snell’s law
slides.body_md: A ray passes from air into a liquid. For one angle of incidence, $\sin i = 0.60$ and $\sin r = 0.45$. Find the refractive index of the liquid with respect to air. Will the ray bend towards or away from the normal?
bullets: Step 1 — $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$.
Step 2 — $n = \dfrac{0.60}{0.45} \approx 1.33$.
Step 3 — n is greater than 1, so the liquid is optically denser than air and the ray bends **towards** the normal.
Check — 1.33 is close to the refractive index of water.

visual.alt: Worked table: sine of i 0.60, sine of r 0.45, refractive index about 1.33

slides.narration: With sine values given, Snell’s law becomes a simple division. Zero point six zero divided by zero point four five is about one point three three. Because this is greater than one, the light slows down in the liquid and bends towards the normal. Comparing your answer with known values is a smart way to check it; this liquid behaves like water.

slides.heading: Quick check: towards or away?
slides.body_md: A ray of light passes from water into air at an angle. What happens to it?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is light going from a denser to a rarer medium, or the other way? Which way does it bend?

slides.heading: Refractive index and the speed of light
slides.body_md: The refractive index tells us how much light **slows down**. The **absolute refractive index** of a medium is $n = \dfrac{c}{v}$, where $c = 3 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$ is the speed of light in vacuum. The refractive index of medium 2 **relative** to medium 1 is $n_{21} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$.

visual.alt: Table of approximate refractive indices of air, water, kerosene, crown glass and diamond

slides.narration: Light zips through a vacuum at three hundred thousand kilometres every second. In water it travels slower, and in diamond slower still. The refractive index compares these speeds. A refractive index of two point four two means light in diamond travels at less than half its speed in vacuum. A higher refractive index means a slower speed and a greater bending of light.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: speed of light in glass
slides.body_md: The refractive index of a glass is 1.5 and that of water is 1.33. Find (a) the speed of light in the glass, and (b) the refractive index of glass with respect to water.
bullets: Step 1 — (a) $v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$.
Step 2 — (b) $n_{gw} = \dfrac{n_g}{n_w} = \dfrac{1.5}{1.33} \approx 1.13$.
Step 3 — Light is slower in glass than in water, so glass is optically denser than water.
Check — the relative index is between 1 and 1.5, as expected for two dense media.

rows: Refractive index of glass relative to water

visual.alt: Worked table: speed of light in glass 2 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second; relative refractive index about 1.13

slides.narration: For the speed, divide the speed of light in vacuum by the refractive index: three times ten to the power eight divided by one point five is two times ten to the power eight metres per second. For the relative refractive index, divide one absolute index by the other. Always ask whether your answer makes sense; a speed faster than light in vacuum would be impossible.

slides.body_md: Solve the numerical question about the speed of light in a medium.
slides.narration: Your turn. Rearrange the refractive index formula to find the speed, and keep the powers of ten tidy.

slides.heading: Optical density is not mass density
slides.body_md: A medium with a **larger refractive index** is **optically denser**: light travels more slowly in it. This is **not** the same as mass density. Kerosene floats on water (lower mass density) but has a **higher** refractive index, so it is optically denser.

visual.alt: Table showing that kerosene is less dense than water by mass but optically denser

slides.narration: Here is a classic trap. Kerosene floats on water, so it has a lower mass density. Yet light travels more slowly in kerosene, so it is optically denser. The words rarer and denser in optics always refer to how fast light travels, never to mass. When a question asks which medium is optically denser, look at the refractive index or the speed of light.

slides.heading: Quick check: optically denser
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about kerosene and water.
slides.narration: Quick check. Separate the two ideas of density in your head before you decide.

slides.heading: Summary: refraction
bullets: Refraction is the change in direction of light when its speed changes at a boundary.
Rarer to denser: bends towards the normal; denser to rarer: away from the normal.
Glass slab: emergent ray parallel to incident ray, with a lateral shift.
Snell’s law: $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n_{21}$ (constant).
Optical density depends on the speed of light, not on mass density.

visual.alt: Summary table of Snell’s law and the absolute and relative refractive index formulas

slides.narration: Let us recap. Light bends when it changes speed at a boundary between two media. Into a denser medium it bends towards the normal; into a rarer one, away. A glass slab returns the ray to its original direction, slightly shifted. Snell’s law gives a constant ratio, the refractive index, which also equals the ratio of the speeds of light.

slides.heading: Exam tips: refraction
bullets: Draw the **normal** as a dashed line at each surface, and mark angles from the normal, not from the surface.
In a slab diagram, show the emergent ray **parallel** to the incident ray and mark i, r and e.
State Snell’s law with "for a given pair of media and a given colour of light".
Write speeds with units (m/s) and powers of ten clearly.
Remember: higher refractive index → lower speed → optically denser.
Typical 3-mark split: laws stated (1) + labelled diagram (1) + calculation or explanation (1).

rows: Angles are measured from the normal
For a slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray
Kerosene is optically rarer because it floats
Optical density depends on the speed of light
n can be less than 1 for glass
Absolute n of any material is greater than 1

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about refraction with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Here are the habits that earn marks. Draw the normal every time and measure angles from it. In the slab diagram, make sure the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. When you state Snell’s law, include the condition about the pair of media and the colour of light. And remember that optical density is all about the speed of light.

slides.heading: Spherical lenses
slides.body_md: Part 4 — how lenses form images, the lens formula, and the power of a lens that opticians write in dioptres.

visual.alt: Flow from a lens to refraction at its surfaces, image formation, the lens formula and power

slides.narration: Spectacles, cameras, microscopes, projectors and your own eyes all use lenses. A lens is simply a piece of glass or plastic with curved surfaces that bends light by refraction. In this final part we learn to find images formed by lenses, calculate their positions with the lens formula, and understand the power printed on a spectacle prescription.

slides.heading: Convex and concave lenses
slides.body_md: A **convex lens** is thicker in the middle; it **converges** parallel rays. A **concave lens** is thinner in the middle; it **diverges** parallel rays.

rows: Lens in spectacles for short sight

visual.alt: Table comparing convex and concave lenses by shape, effect on light, other name and example

slides.narration: Run your finger over a magnifying glass: it bulges in the middle, so it is convex. A convex lens bends parallel rays inwards to meet at a point. A concave lens is thinner in the middle and spreads rays outwards. Each lens has an optical centre, a principal axis, and two foci, one on each side, because light can pass through it either way.

slides.heading: Lens terms and ray rules
slides.body_md: The **optical centre (O)** is the centre of the lens; a ray through O passes **undeviated**. Each lens has two principal foci, **F₁** and **F₂**, at the **focal length f** from O; **2F₁** and **2F₂** are at twice the focal length.

rows: Through F₁ (or towards F₂ for concave)

visual.alt: Table of three standard rays and how convex and concave lenses refract them

slides.narration: Lens ray diagrams use three easy rays. A ray parallel to the axis bends through the far focus of a convex lens, or spreads out as if from the near focus of a concave lens. A ray through the near focus comes out parallel. And a ray through the optical centre goes straight through, without bending. Any two of these rays locate the image.

slides.body_md: Parallel rays from a distant object converge at **F₂**: a real, inverted, **point-sized** image.

slides.narration: With the object exactly at the focus, the lens sends out a parallel beam. The rays never meet, so the image is at infinity. Lighthouses and some torches use this idea with lenses, placing the light source at the focus so the beam travels far without spreading.

slides.narration: Hold a magnifying glass close to small print, closer than its focal length. The letters look big and upright. The rays leaving the lens spread apart, and your eye traces them back to a larger image on the same side as the print. Because the light does not actually come from there, the image is virtual and cannot be caught on a screen.

slides.narration: A concave lens behaves like a convex mirror. Whatever the position of the object, the rays spread out after the lens, and the image is small, upright and virtual, between the focus and the lens. People who cannot see distant objects clearly often wear concave lenses, as you will learn in the next chapter.

slides.heading: The lens formula and magnification
slides.body_md: The same sign convention applies, with the **optical centre** as the origin. The **lens formula** links $u$, $v$ and $f$. Magnification is $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}$ (note: **no minus sign** for lenses). For a **convex** lens $f$ is **positive**; for a **concave** lens $f$ is **negative**.

visual.alt: Table of the signs of focal length, image distance and magnification for convex and concave lenses

slides.narration: Notice two differences from mirrors. The lens formula has a minus sign: one over v minus one over u equals one over f. And magnification for a lens is simply v over u, with no minus sign. A convex lens has a positive focal length because its focus F two is on the far side, where light travels to. A concave lens has a negative focal length.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: convex lens
slides.body_md: An object is placed 18 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 12 cm. Find the position and nature of the image and the magnification.
bullets: Step 1 — Signs: $u = -18\ \text{cm}$, $f = +12\ \text{cm}$.
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{36}$, so $v = +36\ \text{cm}$.
Step 3 — $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{36}{-18} = -2$.
Conclusion — the image is 36 cm on the **other side** of the lens, **real, inverted** and **twice** the size.

slides.narration: Rearrange the lens formula to give one over v equals one over f plus one over u. With u negative, this becomes one over twelve minus one over eighteen, which is one over thirty-six. The image is thirty-six centimetres behind the lens, real because v is positive, and inverted because m is negative. The object is between F one and two F one, exactly as in the diagram.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: concave lens
slides.body_md: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
bullets: Step 1 — Signs: $u = -30\ \text{cm}$, $f = -15\ \text{cm}$.
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $v = -10\ \text{cm}$.
Step 3 — $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-10}{-30} \approx +0.33$.
Conclusion — the image is 10 cm from the lens on the **same side** as the object: **virtual, erect**, about **one third** the size.

rows: Same side as the object: virtual

visual.alt: Worked table: image distance minus 10 centimetres, magnification plus one third

slides.narration: For a concave lens, remember that the focal length is negative. Both terms on the right are then negative, and v comes out negative, so the image is on the same side as the object and virtual. The magnification is positive and less than one: upright and smaller. A concave lens can never give a real image of a real object.

slides.heading: Power of a lens
slides.body_md: The **power** of a lens is its ability to converge or diverge light: $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$, with $f$ in **metres**. The unit is the **dioptre (D)**: $1\ \text{D} = 1\ \text{m}^{-1}$. A **convex** lens has **positive** power; a **concave** lens **negative** power. For lenses in **contact**, the powers **add**: $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$

slides.narration: A strongly curved lens bends light sharply and has a short focal length, so it is more powerful. Power is one divided by the focal length in metres, measured in dioptres. Opticians write a plus sign for convex lenses and a minus sign for concave ones. When lenses are placed together, as in a camera, their powers simply add up.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: power and lenses in contact
slides.body_md: (a) Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 25 cm. (b) A convex lens of power +2.5 D is placed in contact with a concave lens of power −1.0 D. Find the power and focal length of the combination.
bullets: Step 3 — $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} \approx 0.67\ \text{m} = 67\ \text{cm}$; positive, so the combination acts as a **convex** lens.
Check — always convert centimetres to metres before using P = 1/f.

visual.alt: Worked table of lens powers: minus 4 dioptres, plus 2.5, minus 1.0, and the combination plus 1.5 dioptres

slides.narration: The most common slip in power questions is forgetting to convert centimetres into metres. Twenty-five centimetres is zero point two five metres, so the power is minus four dioptres. For lenses in contact, just add the powers with their signs. Plus two point five and minus one give plus one point five dioptres, which means the pair behaves like a convex lens.

slides.heading: Quick check: power and sign
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the power of lenses.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the sign of the focal length of each kind of lens.

slides.heading: Summary: lenses
bullets: Convex lenses converge light; concave lenses diverge it.
Ray rules: parallel → through F₂ (or from F₁); through F₁ → parallel; through O → straight on.
Convex lens images follow the same pattern as a concave mirror; inside F it acts as a magnifier.
Concave lens: always virtual, erect, diminished, between F₁ and O.
Lens formula $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$; $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$.
Power $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$ (f in metres), in dioptres; powers in contact add.

visual.alt: Summary table of the lens formula, magnification and power formulas with their uses

slides.narration: Let us recap. Convex lenses bring light together and can form real or virtual images; concave lenses spread light out and always form small, upright, virtual images. The lens formula has a minus sign, and lens magnification has none. Power, in dioptres, is one over the focal length in metres, and the powers of lenses in contact simply add.

slides.heading: Exam tips: lens problems
bullets: Lens formula: **1/v − 1/u = 1/f**; mirror formula: **1/v + 1/u = 1/f**. Do not mix them up.
Lens magnification is **v/u**; mirror magnification is **−v/u**.
Convex lens: f positive; concave lens: f negative.
Convert cm to m before finding power; state the sign and the unit D.
In lens diagrams, mark O, F₁, F₂, 2F₁, 2F₂, and dash virtual rays.
Typical 3-mark split: signs and formula (1) + v or P (1) + nature of image or type of lens (1).

Concave lens power written as positive

Give the focal length its correct sign for the type of lens. Convert to metres before calculating power, and always end with the sign and the unit, dioptre.

sections.heading: 1. Reflection and spherical mirrors
sections.body_md:
**Laws of reflection:** (1) the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; (2) the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. They apply to all reflecting surfaces. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

A **spherical mirror** is part of a hollow sphere: **concave** if the reflecting surface curves inwards, **convex** if it bulges outwards.

- **Pole (P):** centre of the reflecting surface.
- **Centre of curvature (C):** centre of the sphere of which the mirror is part (in front of a concave mirror, behind a convex one). **Radius of curvature (R) = PC.**
- **Principal axis:** the line through P and C.
- **Principal focus (F):** the point where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex). **Focal length f = PF.**
- For mirrors of small aperture, **R = 2f**.

key_terms.definition_md: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
The point on the axis where parallel rays meet after reflection, or appear to come from.
The diameter of the reflecting surface of the mirror.

sections.heading: 3. Convex mirrors and uses of mirrors
sections.body_md:
A **convex mirror** always forms a **virtual, erect, diminished** image between P and F behind the mirror (at F, point-sized, for an object at infinity).

**Uses:** concave mirrors in **torches, searchlights and headlights** (bulb at F gives a parallel beam), **shaving and make-up mirrors** (enlarged erect image), **dentists' mirrors**, and **solar furnaces** (concentrate sunlight). Convex mirrors as **rear-view (wing) mirrors** of vehicles: always erect, diminished, giving a **wider field of view**.

key_terms.definition_md: The extent of the scene that can be seen in a mirror; larger for a convex mirror.

sections.heading: 4. Sign convention, mirror formula and magnification
sections.body_md:
**New Cartesian sign convention:** the pole is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis; the object is placed to the left; distances in the direction of the incident light are positive and against it negative; heights above the axis are positive and below it negative.

For mirrors: u is negative; f is **negative for concave** and **positive for convex**; v is negative for a real image and positive for a virtual image.

**Magnification** m = h′/h = −v/u. Negative m → real, inverted; positive m → virtual, erect; |m| > 1 enlarged, |m| < 1 diminished. (Derivation of the formula is not required.)

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.

sections.heading: 5. Refraction and its laws
sections.body_md:
**Refraction** is the change in direction of light as it passes obliquely from one medium to another, because its **speed changes**. From a rarer to a denser medium the ray bends **towards** the normal; from denser to rarer, **away** from the normal; along the normal it does not bend.

**Glass slab:** the ray bends towards the normal on entering and away on leaving; the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray** (angle of emergence = angle of incidence) but **laterally shifted**.

**Laws of refraction:** (1) the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (2) for a given pair of media and a given colour of light, sin i / sin r is constant (**Snell's law**). The constant is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

key_terms.definition_md: Change in the direction of light when it passes obliquely from one medium into another.
The sideways displacement of the emergent ray from the line of the incident ray in a glass slab.

sections.heading: 6. Refractive index
sections.body_md:
The **absolute refractive index** of a medium is n = c/v, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum and v its speed in the medium. The **relative refractive index** of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is n₂₁ = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁.

A medium with a larger refractive index is **optically denser** (light travels more slowly in it). Optical density is **not** mass density: kerosene (n = 1.44) floats on water (n = 1.33) but is optically denser.

| Medium | n (approx.) |
|---|---|
| Air | 1.0003 |
| Water | 1.33 |
| Kerosene | 1.44 |
| Crown glass | 1.52 |
| Diamond | 2.42 |

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium.
The medium with the higher refractive index, in which light travels more slowly.

sections.heading: 7. Spherical lenses and the images they form
sections.body_md:
A **convex (converging) lens** is thicker in the middle; a **concave (diverging) lens** is thinner in the middle. Terms: **optical centre O** (rays through it pass undeviated), principal axis, two principal foci **F₁** and **F₂**, focal length **f**, and the points **2F₁**, **2F₂**.

**Ray rules:** parallel to the axis → through F₂ (convex) or appearing to come from F₁ (concave); through F₁ (convex) or towards F₂ (concave) → emerges parallel; through O → straight on.

Convex-lens images follow the table below. A **concave lens** always gives a **virtual, erect, diminished** image between F₁ and O (at F₁ for an object at infinity).

key_terms.definition_md: The central point of a lens; a ray through it passes without deviation.

sections.heading: 8. Lens formula, magnification and power
sections.body_md:
With the optical centre as origin and the same sign convention: f is **positive for a convex lens** and **negative for a concave lens**. For a real image (convex lens) v is positive; for a virtual image v is negative.

**Magnification** for a lens: m = h′/h = v/u (no minus sign).

**Power** P = 1/f with f in **metres**; unit **dioptre (D)**, 1 D = 1 m⁻¹. Convex lenses have positive power, concave lenses negative power. For lenses **in contact**, P = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + …

key_terms.definition_md: The reciprocal of its focal length in metres; a measure of how strongly it converges or diverges light.
The unit of power of a lens: the power of a lens of focal length 1 m.

visual.alt: Table of two example lenses with focal length and power

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using a positive focal length for a concave mirror, or a negative one for a convex lens.
- Mixing up the formulas: mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.
- Writing m = −v/u for a lens (it is v/u) or m = v/u for a mirror (it is −v/u).
- Forgetting to convert centimetres to metres before calculating power.
- Ray diagrams without arrowheads, or virtual rays drawn as solid lines.
- Calling kerosene optically rarer than water because it floats.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, sign, value with unit, or term.
- 2–3-mark numericals: given values with signs and formula (1) + substitution and answer with unit (1) + nature of the image or lens (1).
- Ray diagrams: correct rays with arrows (1) + image located and drawn (1) + position, size and nature stated (1).
- 5-mark answers: often a ray diagram (2) + a numerical (2) + a use or explanation (1).

questions.stem_md: An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. Where is the image, and what is it like?

options.text_md: At F; real, inverted and point-sized
Behind the mirror; virtual, erect and enlarged
Beyond C; real, inverted and enlarged
At C; real, inverted and the same size

questions.solution_md: With the object at C ($u = -2f$), the mirror formula gives $v = -2f$: the image is also at C, real, inverted, and $m = -1$ (same size) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A convex mirror used for security in a shop has a radius of curvature of 2.4 m. What is its focal length?
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{2.4}{2} = 1.2\ \text{m}$ — option (d). (For a convex mirror it is taken as +1.2 m in the sign convention.)

questions.stem_md: For which position of the object does a concave mirror form a virtual image?

options.text_md: At the centre of curvature
Between the focus and the centre of curvature
Beyond the centre of curvature
Between the pole and the principal focus

questions.solution_md: Only when the object is closer than F do the reflected rays diverge, so they appear to meet behind the mirror — option (d). All other positions give real images.

questions.stem_md: A torch maker wants the light from a small bulb to leave the concave reflector as a strong parallel beam. Where should the bulb be placed?

options.text_md: At the principal focus of the reflector
At the centre of curvature of the reflector
Between the focus and the pole
Beyond the centre of curvature

questions.solution_md: Rays from a source at F reflect parallel to the principal axis (the reverse of parallel rays meeting at F) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Rohit holds a large polished steel ladle at arm’s length and looks into its hollow side. Its focal length is only about 4 cm. What does he see?

options.text_md: A large, upright image of his face
A small, upright image of his face
A small, upside-down image of his face
No image at all

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The hollow side is a concave mirror with $f \approx 4$ cm, so C is about 8 cm away.

Step 2 — His face, at arm’s length (about 50 cm), is far beyond C, so the image is real, **inverted and diminished** — option (c).

Step 3 — A small upright image (b) is what he would see in the back (convex) side.

questions.stem_md: Why are convex mirrors used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles?

options.text_md: They always give an enlarged image of vehicles behind.
They form real images that can be seen clearly at night.
They always give an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view.
They make vehicles behind appear closer than they are.

questions.solution_md: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, so a wide area behind fits into a small mirror — option (c). It makes vehicles look smaller and so farther away, not closer (d).

questions.stem_md: The image formed by a convex mirror is always:

options.text_md: real, inverted and diminished
virtual, erect and enlarged
virtual, erect and diminished
real, erect and the same size

questions.solution_md: Reflected rays from a convex mirror always diverge, so the image is virtual, erect and diminished — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Aditi wants to project an enlarged image of a lit candle onto a wall using a concave mirror. Where should she place the candle?

options.text_md: Beyond the centre of curvature
Between the pole and the principal focus
Between the principal focus and the centre of curvature
Exactly at the centre of curvature

questions.solution_md: An image on a wall must be real; real and enlarged needs the object between F and C — option (c). Inside F (b) gives a virtual image that cannot be projected; at C (d) the image is the same size.

questions.stem_md: A mirror never forms an image that can be obtained on a screen, and its image is always smaller than the object, wherever the object is placed. The mirror is:

options.text_md: concave
convex
plane
either concave or plane

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — "Never on a screen" means the image is always virtual, which rules out a concave mirror (a), which forms real images for most positions.

Step 2 — A plane mirror (c) always gives a same-size image.

Step 3 — Always virtual and always smaller fits a convex mirror — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A concave mirror forms an erect image only when the object is placed between its pole and principal focus.

**Reason (R):** Only for this position do the reflected rays diverge, so that they appear to meet behind the mirror and form a virtual image.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. For every other position the rays actually meet in front, giving real, inverted images; inside F they diverge and form a virtual, erect image. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A convex mirror always forms a diminished image.

**Reason (R):** The principal focus of a convex mirror lies in front of the mirror.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the focus of a convex mirror lies behind it — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The image formed by a plane mirror is virtual, erect and the same size as the object.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. It is also laterally inverted and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

questions.stem_md: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the **pole** (P).

questions.stem_md: For a concave mirror, match each object position in Column A with the image position in Column B.

options.text_md: At infinity
Beyond C
Between C and F
Between F and P

questions.solution_md: At infinity → at F (1 → r); beyond C → between F and C (2 → p); between C and F → beyond C (3 → s); between F and P → behind the mirror (4 → q).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the principal focus of a concave mirror.

(b) The radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 24 cm. What is its focal length?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays of light parallel to the axis **meet after reflection** from a concave mirror.

(b) $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ cm.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define F for a concave mirror.

Step 2 — Use $R = 2f$.

questions.stem_md: State one use each of a concave mirror in (a) a vehicle headlight and (b) a dentist’s clinic, and one use of a convex mirror. For each, explain which property of the mirror or its image is being used.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Headlight:** the bulb is placed at the focus of a concave reflector, so the reflected light forms a strong **parallel beam**.

(b) **Dentist:** a concave mirror held close to a tooth (inside F) gives an **enlarged, erect** image, so small details are easy to see.

(c) **Convex mirror:** rear-view mirror of a vehicle, because it always gives an **erect, diminished** image and a **wider field of view**.

questions.solution_md: Link each use to the position of the object and the kind of image or beam produced.
