Dentist: enlarged erect image (object inside F)

questions.stem_md: Draw a ray diagram to show the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed between its principal focus and centre of curvature. State the position, size and nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ray diagram: from the top of the object, one ray **parallel to the axis** reflects through **F**; a second ray **through F** reflects **parallel** to the axis. They meet below the axis beyond C, where the tip of the image is drawn.

Image: **beyond C**, **enlarged**, **real and inverted**.

questions.solution_md: Draw two standard rays with arrows, locate the image where they cross, then describe it.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw ray diagrams to show the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed (i) beyond the centre of curvature and (ii) between the pole and the principal focus.

(b) State the position, size and nature of the image in each case.

(c) Which of these two arrangements is used in a shaving mirror, and why?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) A ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray through F reflects parallel; they meet **between F and C**. (ii) A ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray along the line from C through the object reflects back along itself; the reflected rays **diverge**, and their backward extensions (dashed) meet **behind the mirror**.

(b) (i) Between F and C; **diminished**; **real and inverted**. (ii) Behind the mirror; **enlarged**; **virtual and erect**.

(c) Arrangement (ii): a face held closer than the focus gives an **enlarged, erect** image, which is what a person shaving needs.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Draw two standard rays for each position, with arrows and dashed virtual rays.

Step 2 — Describe each image.

Step 3 — Match the shaving mirror to the enlarged, erect image.

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. Find the image distance v, with its sign, in centimetres.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $u = -20\ \text{cm}$, $f = -12\ \text{cm}$.

Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{20} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$.

Step 3 — $v = -30\ \text{cm}$: the image is 30 cm in front of the mirror (real).

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the magnification produced, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $u = -25\ \text{cm}$, $f = -10\ \text{cm}$: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{25} = -\dfrac{3}{50}$, so $v \approx -16.67\ \text{cm}$.

Step 2 — $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} \approx -\dfrac{-16.67}{-25} \approx -0.67$: real, inverted, diminished.

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance v, with its sign, in centimetres.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $u = -10\ \text{cm}$, $f = +15\ \text{cm}$.

Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.

Step 3 — $v = +6\ \text{cm}$: 6 cm behind the mirror (virtual).

questions.stem_md: A spherical mirror has a radius of curvature of 32 cm. Its focal length is ___ cm.
In the New Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is taken as:

options.text_md: positive, because the mirror converges light
negative, because the focus is in front of the mirror, against the direction of incident light
positive, because the focus is behind the mirror
zero, because the focus lies on the principal axis

questions.solution_md: Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative; the focus of a concave mirror is in front of it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Using the mirror formula for a concave mirror, Sunil finds v = +18 cm. What does this tell him about the image?

options.text_md: It is in front of the mirror, so it is real and inverted.
It is behind the mirror, so it is virtual and erect.
It is at infinity.
He must have made an error, because v is always negative for a concave mirror.

questions.solution_md: A positive v means the image lies behind the mirror, in the direction of the incident light: a virtual, erect image (object inside F) — option (b). Concave mirrors can give positive v (d).

questions.stem_md: A mirror produces a magnification of −0.5. The image is:

options.text_md: real, inverted and half the size of the object
virtual, erect and half the size of the object
real, inverted and twice the size of the object
virtual, erect and twice the size of the object

questions.solution_md: Negative m → real and inverted; size 0.5 → half as tall — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A concave mirror of focal length 10 cm forms a real image twice the size of the object. How far from the mirror is the object?

options.text_md: 5 cm
20 cm
30 cm
15 cm

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Real image, twice the size: $m = -2 = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, so $v = 2u$.

Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{2u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $\dfrac{3}{2u} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$ and $u = -15\ \text{cm}$ — option (d).

Step 3 — Check: $v = -30$ cm, $m = -2$. 5 cm (a) gives a virtual image; 20 cm (b) is at C (same size).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The magnification produced by a convex mirror is always positive and less than 1.

**Reason (R):** A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Erect gives a positive m, and diminished gives a value less than 1, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The focal length of a convex mirror is taken as negative in the New Cartesian sign convention.

**Reason (R):** The focus of a convex mirror lies behind the mirror, in the direction of the incident light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: since the focus is behind the mirror, along the incident light, f is positive. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the New Cartesian sign convention, the distance u of a real object placed in front of a mirror is always negative.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The object is placed to the left, against the direction of the incident light, so u is negative.

questions.stem_md: State the four rules of the New Cartesian sign convention for spherical mirrors.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The **pole** is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis; the object is placed to the **left** of the mirror. (2) Distances measured in the direction of the **incident light** are **positive**. (3) Distances measured **against** the incident light are **negative**. (4) Heights **above** the axis are **positive** and heights **below** are **negative**.

questions.solution_md: List the origin, the two direction rules and the height rule.

questions.stem_md: A 5 cm tall object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the position, nature and height of the image.

answer.model_answer_md:
$u = -30$ cm, $f = -20$ cm, $h = +5$ cm.

$\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = -60$ cm.

$m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-60}{-30} = -2$, so $h' = -2 \times 5 = -10$ cm.

The image is **60 cm in front** of the mirror, **real, inverted** and **enlarged** (10 cm tall).

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — Signs. Step 2 — Mirror formula for v. Step 3 — $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, then $h' = m h$.

questions.stem_md: A dentist uses a concave mirror of focal length 16 cm and wants an erect image of a tooth that is 4 times as large. How far from the tooth should she hold the mirror? Where is the image formed?

answer.model_answer_md:
Erect, so the image is virtual and $m = +4 = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, giving $v = -4u$.

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$: $-\dfrac{1}{4u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{16}$, so $\dfrac{3}{4u} = -\dfrac{1}{16}$ and $u = -12$ cm.

$v = -4u = +48$ cm. She should hold the mirror **12 cm** from the tooth; the image is **48 cm behind** the mirror (virtual, erect).

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — Use m to relate v and u. Step 2 — Substitute in the mirror formula. Step 3 — Find v and interpret.

questions.stem_md:
A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of 60 cm. A 6 cm tall object is placed 20 cm in front of it.

(a) Find the position and size of the image.

(b) State the nature of the image.

(c) Draw a ray diagram for this case.

(d) Give one use of convex mirrors and explain why they suit it.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $f = +\dfrac{60}{2} = +30$ cm; $u = -20$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{12}$, so $v = +12$ cm. $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{12}{-20} = +0.6$, so $h' = 0.6 \times 6 = 3.6$ cm.

(b) **Virtual, erect, diminished**, 12 cm behind the mirror.

(c) A ray parallel to the axis reflects as if coming from F (dashed back to F); a ray aimed at C reflects back along itself (dashed to C); the dashed extensions meet behind the mirror between P and F.

(d) Rear-view mirrors of vehicles: they always give an erect, diminished image and a **wider field of view**.

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — f = R/2, positive for convex. Step 2 — Mirror formula and magnification. Step 3 — Describe and draw. Step 4 — Use with reason.

questions.stem_md:
Priya’s concave make-up mirror has a focal length of 24 cm. She holds her face 16 cm from it.

(a) Calculate the image distance and the magnification.

(b) Describe the image and explain why it is useful for her.

(c) Draw the ray diagram for this situation.

(d) If she moves her face to 60 cm from the mirror, describe the new image without calculation, and say whether it is still useful as a make-up mirror.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $u = -16$ cm, $f = -24$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{1}{48}$, so $v = +48$ cm. $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{48}{-16} = +3$.

(b) The image is **virtual, erect and three times enlarged**, 48 cm behind the mirror: she sees an upright, magnified view of her face.

(c) A ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray along the line from C through the object reflects back on itself; the reflected rays diverge, and their dashed extensions meet behind the mirror.

(d) At 60 cm the face is beyond C (48 cm), so the image is **real, inverted and diminished**, in front of the mirror; it is no longer useful as a make-up mirror.

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — Signs and the mirror formula. Step 2 — Interpret v and m. Step 3 — Ray diagram. Step 4 — Use the position of C (R = 48 cm).

questions.stem_md: A ray of light passes obliquely from water into air. What happens to it at the surface?

options.text_md: It bends away from the normal.
It bends towards the normal.
It passes straight through without bending.
It is always completely reflected back into the water.

questions.solution_md: Light speeds up as it passes from an optically denser medium (water) to a rarer one (air), so it bends away from the normal — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A ray of light passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab. How is the emergent ray related to the incident ray?

options.text_md: It is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
It travels along the same line as the incident ray.
It is perpendicular to the incident ray.
It bends towards the base of the slab at a larger angle.

questions.solution_md: Bending at the first face is reversed at the second, parallel face, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, with a lateral shift — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A pencil dipped slantwise into a glass of water appears bent at the water surface. This is because:

options.text_md: the pencil actually bends in water
light is reflected by the water surface
water absorbs light from the lower part of the pencil
light from the part under water bends as it passes from water into air

questions.solution_md: Rays from the submerged part refract away from the normal as they leave the water, so that part appears raised and the pencil looks bent — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The refractive indices of four materials are: water 1.33, kerosene 1.44, crown glass 1.52 and diamond 2.42. In which material does light travel most slowly?

options.text_md: Water
Diamond
Kerosene
Crown glass

questions.solution_md: Since $v = \dfrac{c}{n}$, the largest refractive index gives the lowest speed: diamond — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Light passes from medium A (refractive index 1.33) into medium B (refractive index 1.65). Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
The light slows down and bends away from the normal.
The light does not bend, because both media are transparent.
The light slows down and bends towards the normal.

questions.solution_md: B has a higher refractive index, so it is optically denser: light slows down and bends towards the normal — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A ray of light falls on a glass surface along the normal (angle of incidence 0°). What happens to it?

options.text_md: It bends towards the normal.
It bends away from the normal.
It is completely reflected.
It passes into the glass without changing direction.

questions.solution_md: With $i = 0$, $\sin i = 0$, so $\sin r = 0$ and $r = 0$: the ray goes straight on (its speed still changes) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The refractive index of a medium is 1.25. Find the speed of light in this medium, in units of 10⁸ m/s. (Speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.)
questions.solution_md: $v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1.25} = 2.4 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.stem_md: For a ray passing from air into a transparent plastic, sin i = 0.50 and sin r = 0.32. Find the refractive index of the plastic, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{0.50}{0.32} \approx 1.56$.

questions.stem_md: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42 and that of glass is 1.50. Find the refractive index of diamond with respect to glass, correct to two decimal places, and say which material is optically denser.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $n_{dg} = \dfrac{n_d}{n_g} = \dfrac{2.42}{1.50} \approx 1.61$.

Step 2 — The value is greater than 1, so diamond is optically denser than glass (light is slower in diamond).

questions.stem_md: Light travels at 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s in a liquid. Find the refractive index of the liquid, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: $n = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{2.25 \times 10^8} \approx 1.33$ (the liquid could be water).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Kerosene is optically denser than water.

**Reason (R):** Kerosene floats on water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but floating depends on mass density, while optical density depends on the speed of light (n = 1.44 for kerosene, 1.33 for water). R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The emergent ray from a rectangular glass slab is parallel to the incident ray.

**Reason (R):** Light travels more slowly in glass than in air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the slower speed explains why light bends, not why the emergent ray is parallel; that is because the two faces are parallel, so the second bending reverses the first — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The absolute refractive index of glass is less than 1.

**Reason (R):** Light travels more slowly in glass than in vacuum.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: n = c/v, and since v in glass is less than c, n is greater than 1. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser, and light travels more slowly in it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True, since n = c/v.

questions.stem_md: For a given pair of media and colour of light, the constant ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the **refractive index** of the second medium with respect to the first (Snell’s law).

questions.stem_md: State the two laws of refraction of light.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence all lie in the **same plane**. (2) For a given pair of media and a given colour of light, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is **constant** (Snell’s law).

questions.solution_md: State both laws, including the conditions in the second.

questions.stem_md: A coin lying at the bottom of a bucket of water appears to be raised when seen from above. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Light from the coin passes from **water into air**, an optically rarer medium, so at the surface it bends **away from the normal**. To an eye above, the rays seem to come from a point higher than the coin, so the coin appears **raised** (the water looks shallower).

questions.solution_md: Trace light from the coin to the eye and apply the rule for denser-to-rarer refraction.

marking_scheme.step: Refraction from water to air, away from the normal
Rays appear to come from a higher point

questions.stem_md: Describe, with the help of a labelled diagram, the path of a ray of light through a rectangular glass slab. Why is the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray?

answer.model_answer_md:
Diagram labels: incident ray, normal at each face, refracted ray inside the slab, emergent ray, angles **i**, **r** and **e**, lateral shift.

On entering the glass the ray slows down and bends **towards** the normal (r < i). On leaving, it speeds up and bends **away** from the normal. Because the two faces are **parallel**, the bending at the second face exactly reverses the bending at the first, so **e = i** and the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray, shifted sideways.

questions.solution_md: Draw the ray with normals and angles; explain the two bendings and why they cancel.

marking_scheme.step: Labelled diagram with normals and angles
Towards then away from the normal
Parallel faces, so e = i and the rays are parallel

questions.stem_md: The refractive index of water is 1.33 and that of a glass is 1.50. (a) Find the speed of light in each. (b) In which is light faster? (c) Which is optically denser?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Water: $v = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1.33} \approx 2.26 \times 10^8$ m/s. Glass: $v = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1.50} = 2.0 \times 10^8$ m/s.

(b) Light is faster in **water**.

(c) **Glass** is optically denser (larger n, lower speed).

questions.solution_md: Use $v = \dfrac{c}{n}$ for each, then compare.

marking_scheme.step: Faster in water; glass optically denser

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is refraction of light? Why does it happen?

(b) State the laws of refraction.

(c) Draw a labelled diagram of refraction through a rectangular glass slab and mark the lateral shift.

(d) The speed of light in a medium is 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Find its absolute refractive index.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Refraction is the **change in direction** of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium into another. It happens because light travels at **different speeds** in different media.

(b) (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. (2) For a given pair of media and colour of light, $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is constant (Snell’s law).

(c) Diagram: incident ray, normals, refracted ray bending towards the normal inside the glass, emergent ray bending away and parallel to the incident ray, angles i, r and e, and the lateral shift between the incident direction and the emergent ray.

(d) $n = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 10^8} = 1.5$.

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — Define and give the cause. Step 2 — Two laws. Step 3 — Labelled slab diagram. Step 4 — n = c/v.

questions.stem_md: Where must an object be placed in front of a convex lens to obtain a real, inverted and diminished image?

options.text_md: At 2F₁
Beyond 2F₁
Between F₁ and 2F₁
Between F₁ and the optical centre

questions.solution_md: An object beyond 2F₁ gives a diminished real image between F₂ and 2F₂ — option (b). At 2F₁ the image is the same size (a); between F₁ and 2F₁ it is enlarged (c); inside F₁ it is virtual (d).

questions.stem_md: A watch repairer uses a convex lens as a magnifying glass. Where must the tiny part of the watch be placed?

options.text_md: Exactly at the focus of the lens
At twice the focal length from the lens
Between the optical centre and the focus of the lens
Beyond twice the focal length from the lens

questions.solution_md: Only an object closer than F₁ gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The image formed by a concave lens of a real object is always:

options.text_md: virtual, erect and diminished
real, inverted and diminished
virtual, erect and enlarged
real, erect and the same size

questions.solution_md: A concave lens diverges light, so its image is always virtual, erect and diminished, between F₁ and O — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 40 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image formed?

options.text_md: 40 cm on the other side of the lens; real, inverted, same size
20 cm on the other side of the lens; real, inverted, diminished
40 cm on the same side as the object; virtual, erect
At infinity

questions.solution_md: The object is at $2F_1$ ($u = -40$ cm $= -2f$). Then $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{1}{40}$, so $v = +40$ cm and $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = -1$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a school projector, a small slide is placed in front of a convex lens so that a large, real image is formed on a distant screen. Where is the slide placed?

options.text_md: Beyond 2F₁
Between F₁ and 2F₁
At F₁
Between F₁ and the optical centre

questions.solution_md: A large real image far away needs the object between F₁ and 2F₁ — option (b). Beyond 2F₁ (a) gives a small image; at F₁ (c) the image is at infinity; inside F₁ (d) it is virtual.

questions.stem_md: A lens forms an erect, diminished image of a distant tree and also an erect, diminished image of a book held close to it. The lens is most likely:

options.text_md: concave
convex
either convex or concave
a thick glass slab

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — A convex lens gives an inverted image of a distant object, and an enlarged image of a close one, so it cannot fit (b).

Step 2 — A concave lens always gives erect, diminished images — option (a). A glass slab (d) does not form diminished images.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ray of light passing through the optical centre of a lens goes straight on without deviation.

**Reason (R):** The optical centre of a lens is the same point as its principal focus.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the optical centre is at the middle of the lens, while the foci are a focal length away on either side — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A convex lens can form a virtual image.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. When the object is between F₁ and O, a convex lens forms a virtual, erect, enlarged image (a magnifying glass).

questions.stem_md: A ray of light passing through the ___ of a lens goes straight on without bending.
questions.solution_md: It is the **optical centre** (O).

questions.stem_md: For a convex lens, match each object position in Column A with the nature of the image in Column B.

options.text_md: Beyond 2F₁
At 2F₁
Between F₁ and 2F₁
Between F₁ and O

questions.solution_md: Beyond 2F₁ → diminished (1 → q); at 2F₁ → same size (2 → s); between F₁ and 2F₁ → enlarged real (3 → p); inside F₁ → virtual erect enlarged (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: Draw a ray diagram to show the image formed by a concave lens of an object placed between F₁ and 2F₁. State the nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ray diagram: a ray **parallel to the axis** is refracted so that it **appears to come from F₁** (dashed back to F₁); a ray **through O** goes straight on. The dashed extension and the ray through O meet **between F₁ and O**, on the same side as the object.

Image: **virtual, erect, diminished**.

questions.solution_md: Two standard rays; locate the image where the ray through O meets the backward extension.

marking_scheme.step: Image between F₁ and O, virtual, erect, diminished

questions.stem_md: Draw a ray diagram for a convex lens with the object placed between F₁ and the optical centre. Describe the image, and name a device that uses this arrangement.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ray diagram: a ray **parallel to the axis** refracts through **F₂**; a ray **through O** goes straight on. The refracted rays **diverge**; their dashed backward extensions meet on the **same side as the object**, beyond it.

Image: **virtual, erect, enlarged**. Device: a **magnifying glass** (simple microscope).

questions.solution_md: Draw the two rays, extend them backwards, describe the image and name the magnifier.

marking_scheme.step: Dashed extensions locate a virtual image on the object’s side

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between a convex lens and a concave lens (two points).

(b) Draw ray diagrams for a convex lens when the object is placed (i) at 2F₁ and (ii) at F₁. State the position and nature of the image in each case.

(c) Explain why a concave lens can never form a real image of a real object.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A convex lens is **thicker at the middle** and **converges** parallel rays; a concave lens is **thicker at the edges** and **diverges** parallel rays.

(b) (i) Ray parallel to the axis → through F₂; ray through O → straight on; they meet at **2F₂**: **real, inverted, same size**. (ii) Ray parallel to the axis → through F₂; ray through O → straight on; the refracted rays are **parallel**, so the image is at **infinity**: real, inverted, highly enlarged.

(c) A concave lens always makes the rays **diverge** after refraction, so they never actually meet; they only appear to meet on the object’s side, giving a **virtual** image.

questions.solution_md: Step 1 — Shape and effect. Step 2 — Two diagrams with descriptions. Step 3 — Divergence means no real meeting point.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Rays always diverge, so the image is virtual

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance v, with its sign, in centimetres.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $u = -15\ \text{cm}$, $f = +10\ \text{cm}$.

Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30}$.

Step 3 — $v = +30\ \text{cm}$: on the other side of the lens (real).

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance v, with its sign, in centimetres.
questions.solution_md: $u = -20$ cm, $f = -20$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{20} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$, so $v = -10$ cm: virtual, on the same side as the object.

questions.stem_md: Find the power of a convex lens of focal length 40 cm, in dioptres.
A convex lens of power +4.0 D is placed in contact with a concave lens of power −1.5 D. Find the focal length of the combination, in centimetres.
An object is placed 10 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the magnification produced.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm.

Step 2 — $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-30}{-10} = +3$: virtual, erect, three times enlarged.

questions.stem_md: An optician’s prescription reads −2.0 D. What kind of lens is it, and what is its focal length?

options.text_md: Convex lens of focal length 50 cm
Concave lens of focal length 50 cm
Concave lens of focal length 2 cm
Convex lens of focal length 2 m

questions.solution_md: Negative power means a concave (diverging) lens. $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-2.0} = -0.5\ \text{m} = -50\ \text{cm}$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which is the correct lens formula in the New Cartesian sign convention?

options.text_md: v − u = f

questions.solution_md: For lenses, 1/v − 1/u = 1/f — option (c). 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (a) is the mirror formula.

questions.stem_md: Which of these lenses converges light most strongly?

options.text_md: A convex lens of focal length 50 cm
A concave lens of focal length 10 cm
A convex lens of focal length 10 cm
A convex lens of focal length 1 m

questions.solution_md: Converging power is largest for the convex lens with the shortest focal length: $P = \dfrac{1}{0.10} = +10\ \text{D}$, compared with +2 D and +1 D; a concave lens diverges light — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The power of a concave lens is negative.

**Reason (R):** The focal length of a concave lens is negative in the New Cartesian sign convention.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
